question.text:
Which of the following are affine transformations?

  1. $\mathbf{T}_1 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} uv \\ u+v \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\mathbf{T}_2 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} v \\ 2v-u \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $\mathbf{T}_3 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} -u^2 \\ 2u+v \end{bmatrix}$
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is not affine since it contains the cross term $uv.$

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_2$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} v \\ 2v-u \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} v \\ -u+2v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 2 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} In fact, the transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is a linear transformation.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_3$ is not affine since it contains the quadratic term $u^2.$

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{T}_2$ only."

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is not affine since it contains the exponential term $e^v.$

Notice that $\mathbf{T}_2$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 8u+2v+2 \\ u-2v+4 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 8u+2v \\ u-2v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 8 & 2 \\ 1 & -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*}

question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is not affine since it contains the quadratic terms $u^2$ and $v^2.$

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_2$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 6v-4u \\ 3u+3v \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -4u+6v \\ 3u+3v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -4 & 6 \\ 3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} In fact, the transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is a linear transformation.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_3$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_3$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} u+v+9 \\ v-9 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} u+v \\ v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -9 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 9 \\ -9 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{T}_2$ and $\mathbf{T}_3$ only."

question.text:
Which of the following are affine transformations?

  1. $\mathbf{T}_1 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 7u-v+6 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix}$
  2. $\mathbf{T}_2 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} 8v-9u \\ 4u-v \end{bmatrix}$
  3. $\mathbf{T}_3 : \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix} \longrightarrow \begin{bmatrix} u-5 \\ 8u \end{bmatrix}$
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

With this in mind, let's look at each transformation in turn.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_1$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_1$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 7u-v+6 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} 7u-v \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 7 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 6 \\ -7 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*}

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_2$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 8v-9u \\ 4u-v \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -9u+8v \\ 4u-v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -9 & 8 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*} In fact, the transformation $\mathbf{T}_2$ is a linear transformation.

  • Transformation $\mathbf{T}_3$ is affine. Notice that $\mathbf{T}_3$ can be expressed as \begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} u-5 \\ 8u \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} u \\ 8u \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 8 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -5 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*}

Therefore, the correct answer is "$\mathbf{T}_1,$ $\mathbf{T}_2,$ and $\mathbf{T}_3.$"

question.text: The matrix form of the affine transformation \[ x = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{a}u+4v, \qquad y = -5u + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{b}v + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{c} \] is shown below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$ \[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -3 & 4 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}+ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

We can carry out the matrix operations using the matrix form, as follows:

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -3 & 4 \\ -5 & 3 \end{bmatrix}}^{A} \cdot \overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}^{\mathbf u}+\overbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}^{\mathbf{b}} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3u+4v \\ -5u+3v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -3u+4v \\ -5u+3v \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

Equating the corresponding elements, we obtain

\[ x = \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{-3}u+4v, \qquad y = -5u + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{3}v + \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{0} \]

Therefore, we have \[ a+b+c = -3+3+0 = 0. \]

What is the value of $a+b+c?$ \[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{a} & 3 \\ \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{b} & -1 \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}+ \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{c} \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

First, notice that we can express the given transformation as \[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3v-8u \\ 3u-v \end{bmatrix}. \]

Separating the constants and expressing the linear part as a product, we get

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} 3v-8u \\ 3u-v \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -8u+3v \\ 3u-v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{-8} & 3 \\ \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{3} & -1 \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{0} \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[ a+b+c = -8+3+0 = -5. \]

example.title: Finding the Matrix Representation of an Affine Transformation Given its Parametric Form

question.text: The matrix form of the affine transformation \[ x = -5v - 2, \qquad y = 7v - 2u - 3 \] is shown below. What is the value of $a+b+c?$ \[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{a} \\ -2 & \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{b} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}+ \begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{c} \\ -3 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
An affine transformation $\mathbf T:\mathbb R^2\rightarrow\mathbb R^2$ is a function of the form \[ \mathbf x = A \mathbf u + \mathbf b, \] where $\mathbf x, \mathbf u,$ and $\mathbf b$ are column vectors in $\mathbb R^2,$ and $A$ is a $2\times 2$ matrix.

First, notice that we can express the given transformation as \[ \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5v-2 \\ 7v-2u-3 \end{bmatrix}. \]

Separating the constants and expressing the linear part as a product, we get

\begin{align*} \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \end{bmatrix} &= \begin{bmatrix} -5v-2 \\ 7v-2u-3 \end{bmatrix} \\[5pt] &= \begin{bmatrix} -5v \\ -2u+7v \end{bmatrix} + \begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}\\[5pt] &= \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 & \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{-5} \\ -2 & \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{7} \end{bmatrix}}_{A} \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf u} + \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} \bbox[Gainsboro,2pt]{-2} \\ -3 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf b}. \end{align*}

Therefore, we have \[ a+b+c = -5+7+(-2) = 0. \]
